item.title: Motivic Cohomology
item.description:
Étale sheaves with transfers

We know that there is a forgetful functor

$$PST(k) \to PShv(Sm/k)$$

which simply allow us to see a presheaf with transfer as a presheaf on the category of smooth schemes. A presehaf with transfers is an étale sheaf with transfers if is an étale sheaf when restricted to the étale site on $Sm/k$. We denote the category of étale sheaves with transfers by $Shv_{ét}(Cor_k)$.

Proposition For any scheme $X$, the presheaf with transfer $\mathbb{Z}_{tr}(X)$ is an étale sheaf with transfers.

Corollary For any étale sheaf with transfers $F$ and any smooth scheme $X$

$$Hom_{Shv_{ét}(Cor_k)}(\mathbb{Z}_{tr}(X), F) = Hom_{PST}(\mathbb{Z}_{tr}(X), F).$$

Corollary For any abelian group the complexes $A(q)$ of presheaves with transfers are complexes of étale sheaves with transfers. In particular, $\mathbb{Z}/n (1)$ is a complex of étale sheaves with transfers quasi-isomorphic to the étale sheaf $\mu_n$.

Proposition Let $\left\{U_i \to X\right\}$ be a Zariski cover. Then the following is exact as a complex of étale sheaves

$$0 \to \mathbb{Z}_{tr}(U_1 \cap \ldots \cap U_n) \to \ldots \to \oplus_i \mathbb{Z}_{tr}(U_i) \to \mathbb{Z}_{tr}(X) \to .O$$

As an application, take the usual covering of $\mathbb{P}^1$. Then there is an exact sequence of complex of étale sheaves

$$0 \to \mathbb{Z}_{tr}(\mathbb{G}_m) \to 2 \mathbb{Z}_{tr}(\mathbb{A}^1,1) \to \mathbb{Z}_{tr}(\mathbb{P}^1,1) \to 0.$$

Since $C_{*}\mathbb{Z}_{tr}(\mathbb{A}^1,1)=0$ we find

$$C_{*}\mathbb{Z}_{tr}(\mathbb{P}^1,1)=C_{*}\mathbb{Z}_{tr}(\mathbb{G}_m)[1]=\mathbb{Z}(1).$$

Moreover, we know we can take the étale sheafification from $PShv(Sm/k)$ to the category of $Sh_{ét}(Sm/k)$. Given $F \in PST(k)$ a presheaf with transfers, we denote $F_{ét}$ the composition of the forgetful functor with the étale sheafification.

Theorem The étale sheaf $F_{ét}$ has a unique structure of an étale sheaf with transfers such that $F \to F_{ét}$ is a morphism of étale sheaves with transfers.

Recall that having transfers is a property! The same actually holds for the Nisnevich topology, but not for the Zariski topology (this will hold if $F$ is $\mathbb{A}^1$-invariant).

Proposition Let $F$ be an étale sheaf with transfers. Then the cohomology presheaves $H^n_{ét}(-,F)$ on $Sm/k$ are preshaeves with transfers.

Contractions

Definition Let $F$ be an homotopy invariant presheaf with transfers. We define $F_{-1}$ as the presheaf with transfers

$$F_{-1}(X) = \textnormal{coker}(F(X \times \mathbb{A}^1) \to F(X \times \mathbb{A}^1 \setminus 0)).$$

item.title: Symmetric Spectra
item.description:
1. The Two Main Objects

The paper constructs and studies two categories:

  • $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ — symmetric spectra of simplicial sets (Sections 1–5)
  • $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma_{\mathcal{T}_*}$ — symmetric spectra of compactly generated topological spaces (Section 6)

The simplicial case is the primary one. Section 6 then lifts the whole theory to the topological setting via geometric realization / singular functor, and the two stable model categories turn out to be Quillen equivalent.

2. What Is a Symmetric Spectrum?

Ordinary spectrum (Definition 1.2.1)

A sequence of pointed simplicial sets $X_0, X_1, \ldots$ together with structure maps $\sigma: S^1 \wedge X_n \to X_{n+1}$.

Symmetric spectrum (Definition 1.2.2)

Same data plus: a basepoint-preserving left action of $\Sigma_n$ on $X_n$ for each $n$, such that the iterated structure map

$$\sigma^p = \sigma \circ (S^1 \wedge \sigma) \circ \cdots \circ (S^{p-1} \wedge \sigma) : S^p \wedge X_n \to X_{n+p}$$

is $\Sigma_p \times \Sigma_n$-equivariant for all $p \geq 1$, $n \geq 0$.

Key slogan: $S^p = (S^1)^{\wedge p}$ carries a left permutation action of $\Sigma_p$; the symmetric spectrum must be compatible with this action at every level.

Note (Remark 1.2.3): It suffices to require equivariance for $\sigma$ and $\sigma^2$ alone (since $\Sigma_p$ is generated by transpositions).

The category of symmetric spectra is denoted $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$; maps are sequences of $\Sigma_n$-equivariant pointed maps commuting with structure maps.

3. The Closed Symmetric Monoidal Structure (§2)

Why ordinary spectra fail

The sphere sequence $S = (S^0, S^1, S^2, \ldots)$ is a monoid in the category of sequences $\mathcal{S}^{\mathbb{N}}_*$, but not a commutative monoid (the twist map on $S^1 \wedge S^1$ is not the identity). Hence there is no closed symmetric monoidal smash product on $\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathbb{N}}$.

Why symmetric spectra work

The sphere symmetric spectrum $S$ is a commutative monoid in the category of symmetric sequences $\mathcal{S}^\Sigma_*$ (Lemma 4.4.1: it is the free commutative monoid on $G_1 S^1$).

Key equivalence (Proposition 2.2.1):

$$\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma \;\simeq\; \text{left } S\text{-modules in } \mathcal{S}^\Sigma_*$$

Smash product (Definition 2.2.3):

$$X \wedge Y := X \otimes_S Y$$

i.e., the relative tensor product over $S$ in the symmetric monoidal category of symmetric sequences.

Main structural theorem (Theorem 2.2.10):

The smash product is a closed symmetric monoidal product on $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$. In particular, there is a natural adjunction isomorphism

$$\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma(X \wedge Y, Z) \cong \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma(X, \mathrm{Hom}_S(Y, Z)).$$

The internal hom $\mathrm{Hom}_S(X,Y)$ is the function spectrum.

4. The Stable Category of Symmetric Spectra of Simplicial Sets

4.1 Stable Equivalence — the critical subtlety (§3.1)

⚠️ Warning: Stable equivalence cannot be defined via stable homotopy groups $\pi_*$ (i.e., via the underlying forgetful functor $U: \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma \to \mathrm{Sp}^{\mathbb{N}}$). The forgetful functor does not preserve stable equivalences.

Definition (3.1.3): A map $f: X \to Y$ is a stable equivalence if $E^0 f: E^0 Y \to E^0 X$ is an isomorphism for every injective $\Omega$-spectrum $E$, where $E^0(X) = \pi_0 \mathrm{Map}(X, E)$.

Equivalently (Proposition 3.1.4), the following are equivalent:

  • $E^0 f$ is an isomorphism for every injective $\Omega$-spectrum $E$
  • $\mathrm{Map}(f, E)$ is a weak equivalence for every injective $\Omega$-spectrum $E$
  • $\mathrm{Hom}_S(f, E)$ is a level equivalence for every injective $\Omega$-spectrum $E$

Important relationship with homotopy groups (Theorem 3.1.11):
If $\pi_* f$ is an isomorphism, then $f$ is a stable equivalence. The converse fails in general (Example 3.1.10: the map $\lambda: F_1 S^1 \to F_0 S^0$ is a stable equivalence but not a $\pi_*$-isomorphism).

Corollary 3.1.8: Every level equivalence is a stable equivalence.

4.2 The Stable Model Structure (§3.4, Theorem 3.4.4)

Main Theorem:

$\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ with the following three classes is a model category:

  • Weak equivalences = stable equivalences
  • Cofibrations = stable cofibrations (= $FI_\partial$-cofibrations = maps with LLP w.r.t. all level trivial fibrations)
  • Fibrations = stable fibrations (= maps with RLP w.r.t. all stable trivial cofibrations)

Key identifications:

  • Stable trivial fibrations = level trivial fibrations (Lemma 3.4.5)
  • Stable fibrations = $J$-injective maps (Corollary 3.4.16)
  • Fibrant objects = $\Omega$-spectra (Corollary 3.4.13), i.e., $X$ such that each $X_n$ is a Kan complex and $X_n \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{Map}(S^1, X_{n+1})$
  • Cofibrant objects: $X$ is stably cofibrant iff $* \to X$ is a stable cofibration; all $F_n K$ are stably cofibrant (Prop. 3.4.2.3)

Characterization of stable cofibrations (Proposition 5.2.2):
$f: X \to Y$ is a stable cofibration iff for all $n \geq 0$, the map

$$\mathrm{Ev}_n(f \square i): X_n \amalg_{L_n X} L_n Y \to Y_n$$

is a $\Sigma_n$-cofibration (i.e., equivariant monomorphism with free $\Sigma_n$-action on new cells), where $L_n X = \mathrm{Ev}_n(X \wedge \bar{S})$ is the latching space.

4.3 Comparison with Bousfield–Friedlander (§4, Theorem 4.3.2)

The forgetful functor $U: \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma \to \mathrm{Sp}^{\mathbb{N}}$ and its left adjoint $V: \mathrm{Sp}^{\mathbb{N}} \to \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ form a Quillen equivalence of stable model categories.

Concretely: $V(X) = S \otimes_{T(G_1 S^1)} GX$. The induced equivalence on homotopy categories identifies $\mathrm{Ho}(\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma)$ with Boardman's stable homotopy category.

The homotopy category of symmetric $\Omega$-spectra $\mathrm{Ho}(\Omega \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma)$ (inverting level equivalences) is also naturally equivalent to Boardman's category (§1.4).

5. Additional Key Properties (§5)

5.1 Two Level Model Structures (Theorem 5.1.2)

There are two model structures with weak equivalences = level equivalences:

  • Projective level structure: cofibrations = stable cofibrations (= $FI_\partial$-cof), fibrations = level fibrations
  • Injective level structure: cofibrations = level cofibrations (= monomorphisms), fibrations = injective fibrations

Corollary 5.1.3: Every symmetric spectrum embeds in an injective spectrum by a level equivalence (enough injectives).

5.2 Monoidal Structure is Compatible (§5.3, Corollary 5.3.8)

Both the projective level structure and the stable model structure on $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ are monoidal: the pushout smash product $f \square g$ of two cofibrations is a cofibration, trivial if either factor is trivial.

Key result (Theorem 5.3.7): if $f$ is an $S$-cofibration and $g$ is a level cofibration, and either is a stable equivalence, then $f \square g$ is a stable equivalence.

Since the sphere spectrum $S$ is cofibrant in $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$, this ensures the smash product descends to a symmetric monoidal structure on $\mathrm{Ho}(\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma)$.

5.3 Proper Model Category (Theorem 5.4.2)

The stable model category of symmetric spectra is proper (both left and right proper).

5.4 The Monoid Axiom (Theorem 5.5.1)

Transfinite compositions of pushouts of maps of the form $f \wedge X$ (where $f$ is a stable trivial cofibration) are stable equivalences.

Consequence (Corollaries 5.5.2–5.5.3): For any monoid $R$ in $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ (= symmetric ring spectrum):

  • There is a model structure on $R$-modules (weak equivalences = underlying stable equivalences)
  • If $R$ is commutative, there is a model structure on $R$-algebras
  • A stable equivalence of monoids $R \xrightarrow{\sim} R'$ induces a Quillen equivalence between module/algebra categories (Theorem 5.5.9)

5.5 Semistable Spectra (§5.6)

A symmetric spectrum $X$ is semistable if $X \to LX$ (fibrant replacement) is a stable homotopy equivalence. Semistable spectra include:

  • All $\Omega$-spectra (fibrant objects)
  • Spectra with finite classical stable homotopy groups
  • Connective spectra satisfying a connectivity growth condition

Proposition 5.6.5: For semistable $X$ and $Y$, a map $f: X \to Y$ is a stable equivalence iff it is a stable homotopy equivalence.

6. The Stable Category of Topological Symmetric Spectra (§6)

6.1 Setup

One works with compactly generated weak Hausdorff spaces $\mathcal{T}_*$ (not all of $\mathrm{Top}_*$, which is not symmetric monoidal under $\wedge$). The category $\mathcal{T}_*$ is a proper monoidal model category.

A topological symmetric spectrum (Definition 6.2.2) is defined exactly as in the simplicial case, replacing simplicial sets by spaces in $\mathcal{T}_*$ and $S^1$ by the unit circle.

Structural equivalence: The category $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma_{\mathcal{T}_*}$ is again equivalent to left $S$-modules (where $S = (S^0, S^1, \ldots)$ with permutation actions), and is a closed symmetric monoidal category.

6.2 Stable Model Structure on Topological Symmetric Spectra (§6.3)

The stable model structure is lifted from the simplicial case via:

  • geometric realization $|\cdot|: \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma \to \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma_{\mathcal{T}_*}$
  • singular functor $\mathrm{Sing}: \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma_{\mathcal{T}_*} \to \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$

Definition (6.3.2): A map $f$ in $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma_{\mathcal{T}_*}$ is:

  • a stable equivalence if $\mathrm{Sing}(f)$ is a stable equivalence in $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$
  • a stable fibration if $\mathrm{Sing}(f)$ is a stable fibration in $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$
  • a stable cofibration if $f$ has LLP w.r.t. all stable trivial fibrations

Theorem 6.3.8: The stable model structure on $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma_{\mathcal{T}_*}$ is a model category. Moreover:

  • $f \in \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ is a stable equivalence $\Leftrightarrow$ $|f|$ is a stable equivalence
  • $g \in \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma_{\mathcal{T}_*}$ is a stable equivalence $\Leftrightarrow$ $\mathrm{Sing}(g)$ is a stable equivalence
  • (Quillen equivalence): $(|\cdot|, \mathrm{Sing})$ is a Quillen equivalence between the stable model structure on $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ and the stable model structure on $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma_{\mathcal{T}_*}$

Fibrant objects = topological $\Omega$-spectra: $X$ such that $X_n \xrightarrow{\sim} X_{n+1}^{S^1}$ for all $n$ (Lemma 6.3.3).

6.3 Properties of the Topological Stable Structure (§6.4)

Monoidal (Corollary 6.4.2): Both the projective level structure and the stable model structure on $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma_{\mathcal{T}_*}$ are monoidal.

Proper (Theorem 6.4.4): The stable model structure on topological symmetric spectra is proper.

Monoids and modules (Theorem 6.4.5): The monoid axiom is unknown for topological symmetric spectra. However:

  • Every monoid $R$ admits a stably cofibrant replacement $R' \xrightarrow{\sim} R$
  • If $R$ is stably cofibrant, there is a model structure on $R$-modules
  • Quillen equivalence holds between module categories under stably cofibrant stable equivalences of monoids

Homotopy category of monoids (Theorem 6.4.6): The homotopy category of monoids in $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma_{\mathcal{T}_*}$ (inverting stable equivalences) is equivalent to the homotopy category of monoids in $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$.

7. Summary Table

Property $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ (simplicial) $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma_{\mathcal{T}_*}$ (topological)
Closed symmetric monoidal ✓ ✓
Stable model structure ✓ (Theorem 3.4.4) ✓ (Theorem 6.3.8)
Fibrant objects $\Omega$-spectra $\Omega$-spectra
Sphere spectrum cofibrant ✓ ✓
Monoidal model structure ✓ (Corollary 5.3.8) ✓ (Corollary 6.4.2)
Proper ✓ (Theorem 5.4.2) ✓ (Theorem 6.4.4)
Monoid axiom ✓ (Theorem 5.5.1) Unknown
Model structure on $R$-modules ✓ for any monoid $R$ ✓ if $R$ stably cofibrant
Quillen equivalent to $\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathbb{N}}$ ✓ (Theorem 4.3.2) ✓ (via composition)
Quillen equivalent to each other — ✓ (Theorem 6.3.8)

Based on: M. Hovey, B. Shipley, J. Smith — "Symmetric Spectra", arXiv:math/9801077 (1998)

item.title: Examples of O-minimality in Algebraic Geometry
item.description:
Based on a YouTube lecture by Hunter Spink. These are informal introductory notes; we do not worry about the details of model theory but focus on the ideas and tools usable in algebraic geometry.

I. Motivation

Algebraic geometry studies sets you can write down using $+$ and $\times$: from these two operations you get all polynomials, and the collection $\{+, \times\}$ is naturally associated to fields.

Question. What if I look at sets defined not just with polynomials, but also using $\sin$, $\cos$, $\exp$, $\log$, ...?

Idea. Model theorists identified the weakest condition on a collection of functions $\mathcal{F}$ that prevents you from creating "bad" sets when you add those functions to your language. "Bad" means: a Cantor set, infinitely many connected components, or a set that is not a piecewise differentiable manifold. The key insight is that the right condition ensures nothing bad can be created at all.

Grothendieck was the first to ask: "Why can't I use $\exp$, $\sin$, $\cos$, ... in geometry?" Nowadays this question has many answers, and o-minimality provides the framework.

II. Definable Sets

The language

Fix a collection of functions $\mathcal{F} = \{+, \times, f_1, \ldots, f_k\}$ where each $f_i : \mathbb{R}^{n_i} \to \mathbb{R}$. Taking $\mathcal{F} = \{+, \times\}$ gives polynomials; in general $\mathcal{F}$ can be any collection.

Remark. The quantifiers $\exists$ and $\forall$ allow us to express the concepts of continuity and differentiability (think of the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition from analysis).

Definition

A set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is $\mathcal{F}$-definable if there exists a first-order formula $\phi(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ such that

$$S = S_\phi := \{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \mid \phi(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \text{ is true}\}.$$

A formula $\phi$ is built from the following ingredients:

Terms (the "nouns"): constants, parentheses, variables, and arbitrary compositions of functions in $\mathcal{F}$, e.g. $f_1(x_2 + f_2(x_1), \sqrt{2})$.

Atomic predicates: $<$, $=$, $>$. Combined with terms, these produce atomic statements such as $f_1(x_2 + f_2(x_1), \sqrt{2}) > f_3(0)$.

Logical connectives: $\lnot$, $\lor$, $\land$, $\to$, $\leftrightarrow$, etc., which combine atomic statements, e.g. $f_1(\cdots) > f_3(0)$ or $f_4(x_1) = f_5(x_2)$.

Quantifiers: $\exists x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, e.g.:

$$\exists\, z \in \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } \bigl(f_1(x_2 + f_2(x_1), \sqrt{2}) > f_3(0)\bigr) \text{ or } \bigl(f_4(x_1, z) = f_5(z)\bigr).$$

Example. With $\mathcal{F} = \{+, \times\}$, the unit circle is definable: it is $S_\phi$ for the formula $\phi(x,y) \equiv (x^2 + y^2 = 1)$.

Examples with $\mathcal{F} = \{+, \times, \exp_\mathbb{R}\}$

The following are all $\mathcal{F}$-definable sets, illustrating how quantifiers let us build new functions from $\exp$ alone:

Graph of a composition:

$$\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid y = e^{e^x(x^2+5x+6)}\} \subset \mathbb{R}^2.$$

A level set with inequality (using $\leq$, which we can write as $< $ or $=$):

$$\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid e^x + e^y \leq 4\} \subset \mathbb{R}^2, \qquad \text{formula: } e^x + e^y = 4 \text{ or } e^x + e^y < 4.$$

An image (using $\exists$):

$$\mathrm{Im}(e^{yz})\big|_{y + e^z = 4} \subset \mathbb{R}, \qquad \text{formula: } \exists\, y, z \in \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } y + e^z = 4 \text{ and } x = e^{yz}.$$

Graph of $e^{(\log x)^2}$ (recovering $\log$ via $\exists$):

$$\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid y = e^{(\log x)^2}\} \subset \mathbb{R}^2, \qquad \text{formula: } \exists\, z \in \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } (e^z = x \text{ and } y = e^{z^2}).$$

Using $\exists z$ with $e^z = x$ is how we define $z = \log x$ without adding $\log$ as a primitive.

Remark. The definable sets for $\mathcal{F} = \{\exp\}$ and $\mathcal{F} = \{\exp, \log\}$ are identical: $\log$ is already definable from $\exp$ via a quantifier.

Power functions are now available: $\{(x,y) \mid y = 5x^\pi\}$ is definable because $5x^\pi = 5 \cdot e^{\pi \log x}$, a composition of $\exp$, $\log$, and constants.

III. O-minimality

Definition. $\mathcal{F}$ is o-minimal if every $\mathcal{F}$-definable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is a finite union of points and intervals (possibly open, closed, or unbounded on either end).

The key word is finite. This is a condition only on subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, but as we will see it has powerful consequences in all dimensions.

What does this constraint rule out?

Example: $\mathcal{F} = \{+, \times, \sin\}$ is NOT o-minimal. The set $S_{\sin(x)=0} = \pi\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}$ is definable (formula: $\sin(x) = 0$), but it is not a finite union of points and intervals. Saying "$\sin$ is not o-minimal" is equivalent to saying: this structure cannot talk about periodic sets without running into infinitely many connected components.

Example: $\mathcal{F} = \{+, \times\}$ IS o-minimal — this is the Tarski–Seidenberg theorem. For every formula $\phi$, there exists a quantifier-free formula $\psi$ (not involving $\exists x \in \mathbb{R}$ or $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$) such that $S_\phi = S_\psi$. This is quantifier elimination for real closed fields, and it implies that every definable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is a finite union of points and open intervals.

As an example of quantifier elimination: $S_{(\exists\, y, z \mid (y-1)^2 + z^2 = x)} = \mathrm{Im}((y-1)^2 + z^2) = (0, +\infty) = S_{0 < x}$.

Known o-minimal structures

$\mathcal{F} = \{+, \times, \exp_\mathbb{R}\}$ is o-minimal — this is a deep theorem requiring hard analysis and model theory.

$\mathcal{F} = \{+, \times, \exp_\mathbb{R},\, \sin\big|_{[0,2\pi]},\, \cos\big|_{[0,2\pi]}\}$ is o-minimal — restricting $\sin$ and $\cos$ to a compact interval removes the periodicity that caused problems above.

The largest known o-minimal structure is the "Pfaffian closure" or "restricted analytic functions."

IV. The Uniform Boundedness Theorem

The fundamental structural result of o-minimality is the following.

Theorem (Uniform Boundedness / Cell Decomposition). If $\mathcal{F}$ is o-minimal, then every definable set $S_\phi \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is a finite Boolean combination of connected differentiable manifolds. Moreover, every $S_\phi$ is homeomorphic to a union of relative interiors of simplices in a finite simplicial complex — so no bad topology is possible.

The deeper "magic" statement is:

For a fixed formula complexity $\mathrm{comp}(\phi) = $ (number of symbols in $\phi$, where constants count as 1 symbol), only finitely many homeomorphism types of simplicial complexes occur. In other words, the topology of $S_\phi$ is bounded purely by the length of the formula defining it, independently of the specific constants appearing.

Corollary 1. Every definable function is piecewise differentiable.

Corollary 2. If $S_\phi$ is a finite set of points, then $|S_\phi|$ is bounded above by a function of $\mathrm{comp}(\phi)$ alone. This corollary is key for applications.

V. First Application: Khovanskii's Fewnomial Theorem

Setup

A polynomial in $m$ variables is written as:

$$f(x_1, \ldots, x_m) = \sum_{(i_1, \ldots, i_m) \in \mathrm{Supp}(f)} a_{i_1 \cdots i_m}\, x_1^{i_1} \cdots x_m^{i_m},$$

where $\mathrm{Supp}(f)$ denotes the set of multi-indices of non-zero coefficients (the support).

Consider a system $\{f_1 = 0, \ldots, f_n = 0\}$ in $(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^n$ with finitely many solutions.

Bézout's theorem gives a bound on the number of solutions in terms of the degrees: $\#\text{solutions} \leq \prod_i \deg(f_i)$. But if the exponents are very large (high degree), this bound becomes terrible.

Claim: there exists a bound independent of the exponents, depending only on the sizes of the supports.

Theorem (Khovanskii's Fewnomial Theorem). If the system $\{f_1 = 0, \ldots, f_n = 0\}$ has finitely many solutions in $(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^n$, then the number of solutions is bounded by a function of $|\mathrm{Supp}(f_1)|, \ldots, |\mathrm{Supp}(f_n)|$ alone.

Proof via o-minimality

The key observation is how to encode the system without increasing the number of symbols as the exponents grow. Note that:

$$x^2 + xy = e^{2\log x} + e^{\log x + \log y}, \qquad x^n + xyz = e^{n\log x} + e^{\log x + \log y + \log z}.$$

Even replacing 2 by $n$ (a large exponent), the number of symbols in the formula does not change — the exponent $n$ appears as a constant, which counts as 1 symbol. Rewriting the system using $\exp$ and $\log$:

$$\phi(x_1, \ldots, x_m)\colon \sum_{(i_1,\ldots,i_m)\in\mathrm{Supp}(f_1)} a_{i_1\cdots i_m}\, \exp(i_1\log x_1 + \cdots + i_m\log x_m) = 0 \quad \land \quad \cdots$$

The complexity $\mathrm{comp}(\phi)$ depends only on the number of non-zero coefficients $|\mathrm{Supp}(f_j)|$, not on the size of the exponents. By Corollary 2 above (and the fact that $\mathcal{F} = \{+, \times, \exp\}$ is o-minimal), the number of solutions is bounded by a function of $\mathrm{comp}(\phi)$, which is a function of the support sizes. $\square$

VI. Second Application: Pila–Wilkie Point Counting

Setup

A semi-algebraic set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is defined by polynomial equations and inequalities (e.g. curves, parabolas, discs). Semi-algebraic sets can contain many rational points: for example, $\{(x,y) \mid y = x^2\} \cap \mathbb{Q}^2$ is infinite.

Surprisingly, transcendental sets contain very few rational points.

Definition. For $S \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, the transcendental part of $S$ is:

$$S_{\mathrm{tr}} := S \setminus \bigcup\{V \mid V \subset S \text{ semi-algebraic},\, \dim V \geq 1\},$$

i.e. we remove all positive-dimensional semi-algebraic subsets contained in $S$ — everything that is not "algebraic geometry."

Define the height of a rational point $(a_1/b_1, \ldots, a_n/b_n) \in \mathbb{Q}^n$ (with $a_i, b_i \in \mathbb{Z}$) to be $\max(|a_i|, |b_i|)$.

Theorem (Pila–Wilkie). Let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be definable over an o-minimal structure $\mathcal{F} = \{+, \times, \ldots\}$. Then

$$\#\!\left\{\left(\tfrac{a_1}{b_1}, \ldots, \tfrac{a_n}{b_n}\right) \in S_{\mathrm{tr}} \cap \mathbb{Q}^n \;\middle|\; |a_1|, \ldots, |a_n|, |b_1|, \ldots, |b_n| \leq N\right\}$$

grows slower than $N^\varepsilon$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$.

In other words, the count grows slower than any polynomial in $N$ (slower than $N^{1/2}$, $N^{1/3}$, ...). The only hypothesis needed is that $S$ is definable!

The o-minimality restricts the possible number of rational points in the transcendental part. This is a shocking theorem.

VII. Application of Pila–Wilkie: Multiplicative Manin–Mumford

Statement

Let $f(x, y) = \sum a_{jk} x^j y^k$ be an irreducible polynomial with $|\mathrm{Supp}(f)| \geq 3$.

Theorem (Multiplicative Manin–Mumford). There are only finitely many solutions to $f(x, y) = 0$ with $x, y$ roots of unity.

Why is this surprising? Each individual root of unity $e^{2\pi i/n}$ is algebraic, but there is no way to put all of them together into a single algebraic family — the "reason" for the finiteness is transcendental.

Reformulation

For $z \in \mathbb{C}$, set $\omega(z) = e^{2\pi i z}$. The theorem is equivalent to: there are finitely many solutions $(s,t) \in (\mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1])^2$ to $f(\omega(s), \omega(t)) = 0$.

Proof via Pila–Wilkie

Step 1: The structure $\mathcal{F} = \{+, \times, \exp_\mathbb{R}, \cos(2\pi x)|_{[0,1]}, \sin(2\pi x)|_{[0,1]}\}$ is o-minimal.

Step 2: Define the surface. Note that $\omega(a+ib) = e^{-b}\cos(2\pi a) + ie^{-b}\sin(2\pi a)$, so

$$S := \{(s,t) \in \mathbb{C}^2 \cong \mathbb{R}^4 \mid 0 \leq \mathrm{Re}(s), \mathrm{Re}(t) \leq 1 \text{ and } f(\omega(s), \omega(t)) = 0\}$$

is a definable set over $\mathcal{F}$ (and a complex surface), sitting inside $(\mathbb{R} + i\mathbb{R})^2 \cong \mathbb{R}^4$.

Step 3: The transcendental part. One shows that $S = S_{\mathrm{tr}}$, i.e. $S$ contains no positive-dimensional semi-algebraic subsets (intuitively: $f$ is irreducible and transcendental, so its zero set on $[0,1]^2$ cannot contain any algebraic curve). This uses the irreducibility of $f$ and the condition $|\mathrm{Supp}(f)| \geq 3$.

Step 4: Apply Pila–Wilkie. The rational points of $S \cap \mathbb{Q}^4$ of height $\leq N$ correspond precisely to solutions $(\omega(p/q), \omega(r/s))$ with $q, s \leq N$ — i.e., roots of unity of order $\leq N$. By Pila–Wilkie, their count is $O(N^\varepsilon)$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$.

Step 5: Contradiction via Galois. Suppose $f(\omega(3/124), \omega(a/b)) = 0$ with $124 \nmid b$. Applying Galois automorphisms (which permute the roots of unity), we get solutions $(\omega(i/124), \omega(a'/b))$ for all $1 \leq i \leq 124$ with $\gcd(i, 124) = 1$. There are at least $\sqrt{124}$ such values, giving at least $\sqrt{124}$ points on $S$ of height $\leq 124$. More generally, if we had infinitely many root-of-unity solutions as $N \to \infty$, the count would grow at least polynomially (like $\sqrt{N}$), contradicting the Pila–Wilkie bound of $O(N^\varepsilon)$.

Therefore there are only finitely many root-of-unity solutions to $f(x,y) = 0$. $\square$

item.title: Exponential Motives — Lesson IV
item.description:
Recap

We are working with $k \subset \mathbb{C}$, $X$ a smooth variety over $k$, and $f: X \to \mathbb{A}^1_k$ a global regular function. Setting $f = 0$ recovers the usual theories; we will see that this can happen for $f \neq 0$ as well.

Twisted de Rham cohomology:

$$H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, f) = \mathbb{H}^n_{\mathrm{Zar}}\!\left(X,\; \mathcal{O}_X \xrightarrow{d_f} \Omega^1_X \xrightarrow{d_f} \cdots\right), \qquad d_f(\omega) = d\omega - df \wedge \omega.$$

Rapid decay homology (relative version): given $Y \subset X$ a closed subvariety,

$$H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_*(X, Y, f) := \varinjlim_{r \to +\infty} H_*\!\left(X(\mathbb{C}),\; Y(\mathbb{C}) \cup f^{-1}(S_r);\; \mathbb{Q}\right),$$

where $S_r = \{\mathrm{Re}(z) > r\}$. The subvariety $Y$ allows boundaries to land in $Y(\mathbb{C})$, in addition to the usual rapid decay region. The transition maps are eventually isomorphisms (by the same Zariski open / homotopy equivalence argument as before). The twisted de Rham version $H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, Y, f)$ can be defined analogously; we will see it in the examples.

I. Rapid Decay Cohomology

Definition. The rapid decay cohomology is the linear dual of rapid decay homology:

$$H^*_{\mathrm{Rd}}(X, Y, f) := \mathrm{Hom}_\mathbb{Q}\!\left(H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_*(X, Y, f),\; \mathbb{Q}\right) = \varinjlim_{r \to +\infty} H^*\!\left(X(\mathbb{C}),\; Y(\mathbb{C}) \cup f^{-1}(S_r)\right).$$

The transition maps are eventually isomorphisms for the same reason as in the $Y = \emptyset$ case.

II. Properties

(1) Functoriality

Given a morphism $h: X \to X'$ with $f = f' \circ h$ and $h(Y) \subset Y'$, the map $h$ sends the pair $(X(\mathbb{C}),\; Y(\mathbb{C}) \cup f^{-1}(S_r))$ to $(X'(\mathbb{C}),\; Y'(\mathbb{C}) \cup (f')^{-1}(S_r))$. Passing to the colimit gives a pullback map:

$$h^*: H^*_{\mathrm{Rd}}(X', Y', f') \longrightarrow H^*_{\mathrm{Rd}}(X, Y, f).$$

(2) Boundary Morphisms

For a triple $Z \subset Y \subset X$, the inclusion of pairs gives a map $H^*_{\mathrm{Rd}}(X, Y, f) \to H^*_{\mathrm{Rd}}(X, Z, f)$. The boundary morphism goes in the other direction in homology — if the boundary of a chain can lie in $Z$ it can certainly lie in $Y$ — so in cohomology it goes:

$$\cdots \to H^{n-1}(Y, Z, f|_Y) \to H^n(X, Y, f) \to H^n(X, Z, f) \to \cdots$$

Think in homology first to get the direction right, then dualize.

Exercise. This is a long exact sequence. Prove it using the long exact sequence for triples:

$$Z(\mathbb{C}) \cup f^{-1}(S_r) \;\subset\; Y(\mathbb{C}) \cup f^{-1}(S_r) \;\subset\; X(\mathbb{C}).$$

(3) Künneth Formula

Given two triples $(X, Y, f)$ and $(X', Y', f')$, define the Thom–Sebastiani sum:

$$f \boxplus f': X \times X' \longrightarrow \mathbb{A}^1_k, \qquad (x, x') \longmapsto f(x) + f'(x').$$

Then there is a Künneth isomorphism:

$$H^*_{\mathrm{Rd}}\!\left(X \times X',\; Y \times X' \cup X \times Y',\; f \boxplus f'\right) \simeq H^*_{\mathrm{Rd}}(X, Y, f) \otimes H^*_{\mathrm{Rd}}(X', Y', f').$$

III. The Comparison Isomorphism

Theorem (Deligne; Bloch–Esnault; Hien–Roucairol). There is a canonical isomorphism

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, f) \otimes_k \mathbb{C} \xrightarrow{\sim} H^*_{\mathrm{Rd}}(X, f) \otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{C},$$

dual to a perfect pairing

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, f) \otimes H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_*(X, f) \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}.$$

When $X$ is affine, the de Rham side is computed from global sections, and the pairing is:

$$\left([\omega],\; \sigma = (\sigma_r)_r\right) \longmapsto \int_\sigma e^{-f}\omega := \lim_{r \to +\infty} \int_{\sigma_r} e^{-f}\omega.$$

Here $(\sigma_r)_r$ is the compatible system of chains defining the rapid decay cycle: each $\sigma_r \in C_n(X(\mathbb{C}))$ satisfies $\partial\sigma_r \subset f^{-1}(S_r)$. The integral $\int_{\sigma_r} e^{-f}\omega$ converges because $e^{-f}$ decays exponentially on $\{\mathrm{Re}(f) > r\}$ — this is precisely the rapid decay condition! Therefore the limit is well-defined.

Remark (novelty of the proof). The key subtlety is that the natural map

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, f) \longrightarrow H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X^{\mathrm{an}}, f^{\mathrm{an}})$$

is NOT an isomorphism in general. This is the essential difference from the classical case.

Recall: a connection $\mathcal{E} \xrightarrow{\nabla} \mathcal{E} \otimes \Omega^1_X$ has regular singularities at infinity if $\mathcal{E}$ extends to a coherent sheaf $\bar{\mathcal{E}}$ on a compactification $\bar{X}$, and $\nabla$ extends to

$$\bar{\mathcal{E}} \xrightarrow{\bar\nabla} \bar{\mathcal{E}} \otimes \Omega^1_{\bar{X}}(\log D),$$

independently of the choice of compactification $\bar{X}$ (where $D = \bar{X} \setminus X$).

Theorem (Deligne). If $(\mathcal{E}, \nabla)$ has regular singularities, then:

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, (\mathcal{E}, \nabla)) \otimes_k \mathbb{C} \simeq H^*(X(\mathbb{C}),\; \ker(\nabla^{\mathrm{an}}))$$

(cohomology of the associated local system).

Main point. The connection $(\mathcal{O}_X, \nabla_f)$ with $\nabla_f(1) = -df$ does not have regular singularities in general. For example, take $X = \mathbb{A}^1_k$ and $f = x$: the compactification is $\mathbb{P}^1$, and in the coordinate $t = 1/x$ at infinity we get $dx = d(1/t) = -t^{-2}\,dt$, which has a double pole at $\infty$. So the connection cannot extend with only logarithmic poles. This is the phenomenon of irregular singularities, and it is precisely what makes the algebraic and analytic de Rham cohomologies differ.

IV. Definition of Exponential Periods

Definition. Let $k \subset \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. An exponential period is a coefficient of the comparison isomorphism for some $H^n(X, Y, f)$, i.e. a number of the form

$$[\omega] \otimes [\sigma] \longmapsto \int_\sigma e^{-f}\omega$$

for $[\omega] \in H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, Y, f)$, $[\sigma] \in H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_n(X, Y, f)$, and $(X, Y, f)$ defined over $k$.

V. Examples

Example (0): $f$ constant

If $f$ is constant, $d_f = d$ and the twisted de Rham complex is the usual one, so:

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, f) = H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X), \qquad H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_*(X, f) = H^B_*(X).$$

However, the comparison isomorphism is different: the pairing gives $\int_\sigma e^{-f}\omega = e^{-f} \int_\sigma \omega$, so the period matrix is multiplied by the constant $e^{-f}$. For $f = 0$ we recover the usual pairing; for $f \neq 0$ everything is multiplied by $e^{-f}$.

Concrete example. Take $\alpha \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, $X = \mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Q}(\alpha))$ (a point), and $f = -\alpha \in \mathcal{O}(X) = \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$. The pairing is evaluation at the point, giving $e^\alpha$. Therefore:

$$e^\alpha \text{ is an exponential period of } (X, f).$$

Conjecture. $e^\alpha$ is not a (classical) period — it is transcendental over the field generated by all classical periods. In particular, exponential periods are algebraically independent from classical periods as one varies $\alpha$.

Remark. This is "impossible to prove at the moment" in general. However, we have the following powerful result in this direction:

Theorem (Hermite–Lindemann–Weierstrass). Let $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ be $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent. Then $e^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, e^{\alpha_n}$ are algebraically independent over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. That is, if $p \in \mathbb{Q}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ satisfies $p(e^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, e^{\alpha_n}) = 0$, then $p = 0$.

Remarks.

  • We do not know 3 classical periods that are algebraically independent over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.
  • For exponential periods we can get as many algebraically independent ones as we want, from the theorem above.
  • More precisely: $\mathrm{tr.deg}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(e^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, e^{\alpha_n}) = \mathrm{rank}_\mathbb{Q}\langle\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n\rangle$. If the $\alpha_i$ are $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent, this is exactly $n$.

Example (1): $X = \mathbb{A}^1_k$, $f = x^n$, $n \geq 2$

We already computed:

$$H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^1, x^n) = \mathbb{Q}[dx], \qquad H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_1(\mathbb{A}^1, x^n) = \mathbb{Q}[\mathbb{R}]$$

(one generator each, as seen in the previous lecture).

The pairing gives $\int_\mathbb{R} e^{-x^n}\,dx = \sqrt{\pi}$ for $n = 2$. So:

$$\sqrt{\pi} = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-x^2}\,dx \quad \text{is an exponential period.}$$

Since $\pi$ is a classical period (of $(\mathbb{G}_m, \emptyset, 0)$ for example), $\sqrt{\pi}$ is algebraic over the ring of classical periods — unlike $e^\alpha$ above. This illustrates the difference between the two types of exponential periods.

Proof that $\sqrt{\pi}^2 = \pi$: we want to verify that $\left(\int_\mathbb{R} e^{-x^2}\,dx\right)^2 = \pi$, i.e. $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-x^2-y^2}\,dx\,dy = \pi$.

By the Künneth formula with the Thom–Sebastiani sum:

$$H^1(\mathbb{A}^1, x^2)^{\otimes 2} = H^2(\mathbb{A}^2, x^2+y^2), \qquad dx \otimes dy \longmapsto dx\,dy,$$

and $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a valid rapid decay 2-cycle (its boundary lies in $\{\mathrm{Re}(x^2+y^2) > r\}$ for each $r$, since at each step we can take a large disc whose boundary circle lies in that region). Computing in polar coordinates:

$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,dx\,dy = \left(\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2} r\,dr\right)\left(\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta\right) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2\pi = \pi.$$

Technical point. The naive change of variables to polar coordinates uses $\sin$ and $\cos$, which are not algebraic. The algebraic way to handle this is to introduce the unit circle $C: s^2 + t^2 = 1$ (whose points play the role of $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$) and the map:

$$h: \mathbb{A}^1 \times C \longrightarrow \mathbb{A}^2, \qquad (r, (s,t)) \longmapsto (rs, rt).$$

This is algebraic and gives the change of variables. The function on $\mathbb{A}^1 \times C$ is $r^2 \boxplus 0$ (Thom–Sebastiani sum with the zero function on $C$), which maps to $x^2 + y^2$ on $\mathbb{A}^2$.

The induced map on cohomology is:

$$h^*: H^2(\mathbb{A}^2, x^2+y^2) \longrightarrow H^2(\mathbb{A}^1 \times C, \{0\} \times C, r^2 \boxplus 0)$$

By Künneth: $H^2(\mathbb{A}^1 \times C, \{0\} \times C, r^2 \boxplus 0) \simeq H^1(\mathbb{A}^1, \{0\}, r^2) \otimes H^1(C)$. Computing this:

$$dx\,dy \longmapsto d(rs)\otimes d(rt) = (r\,ds + s\,dr)\otimes(r\,dt + t\,dr) = r\,dr \otimes (s\,dt - t\,ds) + \ldots$$

The terms $ds \otimes dt$ and $dr \otimes dr$ vanish. The surviving term is $r\,dr \otimes (s\,dt - t\,ds)$. But $r\,dr = 0$ in $H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^1, r^2)$: this follows because $d_f(-1/2) = -r^2 \cdot (-1/2) \cdot 2r\,dr = r\,dr$ wait — more precisely, $d_f(-1/2) = d(-1/2) - df \wedge (-1/2) = 0 - 2r\,dr \cdot (-1/2) = r\,dr$, so $r\,dr = 0$ in the cokernel. Therefore $h^*$ is the zero map:

$$h^*: H^2(\mathbb{A}^2, x^2+y^2) \longrightarrow H^1(\mathbb{A}^1, r^2) \otimes H^1(C) = 0.$$

Why does this not contradict the computation? Because $\mathbb{R}$ is a valid rapid decay cycle for $r^2$, but $[0, +\infty)$ is not — a chain from $0$ to $\infty$ does not have its boundary in the rapid decay region (the boundary includes $\{0\}$, which is not in $\{\mathrm{Re}(r^2) > r_0\}$). This is why the change of variables is "not allowed" at the level of rapid decay cycles: $\mathbb{R}$ is a cycle, but $(0, +\infty)$ is not.

Resolution via a subvariety. To make the Künneth argument work, we introduce $Y = \{0\} \subset \mathbb{A}^1$ and use the long exact sequence. For $X = \mathbb{A}^1$, $Y = \{0\}$, $f = x^2$:

$$H^1(\mathbb{A}^1, \{0\}, x^2) \longrightarrow H^1(\mathbb{A}^1, x^2) \longrightarrow 0$$

and from the long exact sequence:

$$H^0(Y, f|_Y) = H^0(\{0\}, 0) = H^0(\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Q})) = \mathbb{Q}(0)$$

(where $(0)$ means the constant function zero on $Y = \{0\}$). In fact $H^1(\mathbb{A}^1, \{0\}, x^2) \simeq H^1(\mathbb{A}^1, x^2) \oplus \mathbb{Q}(0)$ as a direct sum.

Now using $\{0\} \times C \subset \mathbb{A}^1 \times C$, the map $h$ sends $\{0\} \times C$ to $\{(0,0)\} \subset \mathbb{A}^2$, and in the relative setting:

$$H^2(\mathbb{A}^2, \{(0,0)\}, x^2+y^2) \simeq H^2(\mathbb{A}^2, x^2+y^2)$$

(the point does not change things). By Künneth:

$$H^2(\mathbb{A}^1 \times C, \{0\} \times C, r^2 \boxplus 0) \simeq H^1(\mathbb{A}^1, \{0\}, r^2) \otimes H^1(C) \simeq \bigl(\mathbb{Q}(0) \oplus H^1(\mathbb{A}^1, r^2)\bigr) \otimes H^1(C).$$

The projection onto the $\mathbb{Q}(0) \otimes H^1(C) = H^1(C)$ component is the key piece. Total result:

$$h^*: H^2(\mathbb{A}^2, x^2+y^2) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^1(C).$$

The generator $dx\,dy$ maps to $s\,dt - t\,ds$ (the angular form on $C$, i.e. $d\theta$ in disguise), which is a generator of $H^1(C)$. This is an isomorphism.

Upshot. We have proved:

$$H^1(\mathbb{A}^1, x^2)^{\otimes 2} \simeq H^2(\mathbb{A}^2, x^2+y^2) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^1(C) = H^1(\{x^2+y^2=1\}).$$

This is a classical motive — the cohomology of the affine conic $C$.

Remarks. (a) If $k$ contains $\sqrt{-1}$, then $x^2 + y^2 = (x+iy)(x-iy)$, so $C \simeq \mathbb{G}_m$ and $H^1(C) \simeq \mathbb{Q}(-1)$ (the Tate twist, since $H^1_B(\mathbb{G}_m) = \mathbb{Q}(-1)$ is a pure Hodge structure of weight 2, Hodge type $(1,1)$).

(b) The period we found is $\pi$, not $2\pi i$. Note that $2\pi i = \pi \cdot (2i)$, and $2i$ is an algebraic number, so $2\pi i$ is just a period times an algebraic number — consistent with what we found.

The compactification $C \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$ (via $x^2 + y^2 = z^2$) has $D = \mathbb{P}^1 \setminus C = \mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Q}(i))$, two points, explaining the structure.

Goal. Understand when an exponential motive is isomorphic to a classical motive. We will approach this with the same Nori motive machinery.

Example (2): $X = \mathbb{G}_m$, $f = x + 1/x$

The variety is $X = \mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Q}[x, x^{-1}])$, affine, so we compute twisted de Rham from global sections:

$$\mathbb{Q}[x, x^{-1}] \xrightarrow{d_f} \mathbb{Q}[x, x^{-1}]\,dx, \qquad P \longmapsto \left(P'(x) - \left(1 - \frac{1}{x^2}\right)P(x)\right)dx.$$

Claim:

$$H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{G}_m, f) = \mathbb{Q}\!\left[\frac{dx}{x}\right] \oplus \mathbb{Q}[dx].$$

Proof that these two are linearly independent. Suppose $a + b/x = P'(x) - (1 - 1/x^2)P(x)$ has a solution $P \in \mathbb{Q}[x, x^{-1}]$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Q}$. Looking at the recursion on Laurent coefficients one shows this is impossible (exercise: verify this by writing $P = \sum c_n x^n$ and checking that the system of equations for the $c_n$ has no solution).

Remark. More generally, $\mathbb{Q}[x^{n+1}\,dx] \oplus \mathbb{Q}[x^n\,dx]$ spans the cokernel (one can reduce any monomial to lower degree using $d_f$).

Rapid decay homology. The function $f = x + 1/x$ on $\mathbb{C}^*$ has $\mathrm{Re}(f) \to +\infty$ in two directions: along the positive real axis $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ (as $x \to +\infty$ or $x \to 0^+$), and along the circle $|x|=1$ the function is purely imaginary and does not grow. The two rapid decay generators of $H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_1(\mathbb{G}_m, f)$ are:

  • The unit circle $\bigcirc$ (a cycle, boundary empty);
  • The positive real line $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ (boundary $\{0\}$ and $\{\infty\}$, which are in the rapid decay region for large $r$).
$$H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_1(\mathbb{G}_m, f) = \mathbb{Q}\!\left[\bigcirc\right] \oplus \mathbb{Q}\!\left[\mathbb{R}_{>0}\right].$$

Period matrix. The interesting entry is the integral over the unit circle:

$$\oint_{|x|=1} e^{-(x+1/x)}\frac{dx}{x} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \oint_{|x|=1} \frac{(-1)^n}{n!}\left(x + \frac{1}{x}\right)^n \frac{dx}{x} = 2\pi i \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{2^{2n} \cdot n!} \cdot \frac{(-1)^n \cdot 2^{2n}}{n!}$$

Working this out carefully (using the residue of $(x + 1/x)^n/x$ at $x=0$, which picks out the $x^0$ coefficient):

$$\oint_{|x|=1} e^{-(x+1/x)}\frac{dx}{x} = 2\pi i \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{(2n)!} \cdot (-1)^n \cdot 2^{2n}$$

which simplifies to:

$$= 2\pi i \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{(n!)^2} = 2\pi i \cdot I_0(2) \qquad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{this is an exponential period.}$$

More generally, turning this into a function of a parameter $z$:

$$z \longmapsto \int_\sigma e^{-z(x+1/x)}\frac{dx}{x} = 2\pi i \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{z^{2n}}{((2n)!/\binom{2n}{n})} = 2\pi i \cdot I_0(2z),$$

where $I_0$ is the modified Bessel function of the first kind:

$$I_0(2z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{z^{2n}}{(n!)^2},$$

important in physics. It satisfies a differential equation (Bessel's equation), which reflects the Gauss–Manin connection on the cohomology bundle.

The exponential factor in the integrand is what allows these transcendental series — algebraically non-trivial numbers — to appear as periods of a simple algebraic variety.

Another example: exponential motives that are classical

Claim. For any $(X, f)$, the cohomology $H^*(X \times \mathbb{A}^1, z \cdot f)$ (where $z$ is the coordinate on $\mathbb{A}^1$ and the function is $(x, z) \mapsto z \cdot f(x)$) is a classical motive — isomorphic to usual cohomology (without a function) using only the three relations (bilinearity, change of variables, Stokes).

Intuition from $\mathbb{F}_p$. Working over $\mathbb{F}_p$, fix a non-trivial additive character $\psi: (\mathbb{F}_p, +) \to (\mathbb{C}^\times, \cdot)$, e.g. $\psi(x) = e^{2\pi i x/p}$. The exponential sum:

$$\sum_{x \in X(\mathbb{F}_p),\; z \in \mathbb{F}_p} \psi(z \cdot f(x))$$

is a generalization of point counting ($\psi = 1$ gives $\#X(\mathbb{F}_p)$). Setting $W = X \times \mathbb{A}^1$, $g = z \cdot f$:

$$\sum_{x \in X(\mathbb{F}_p),\; z \in \mathbb{F}_p} \psi(z \cdot f(x)) = \sum_{\substack{x \in X(\mathbb{F}_p),\; z \in \mathbb{F}_p \\ f(x) \neq 0}} \psi(z \cdot f(x)) + p \cdot \#\{f=0\}(\mathbb{F}_p).$$

By orthogonality of characters, $\sum_{z \in \mathbb{F}_p} \psi(z \cdot f(x)) = 0$ whenever $f(x) \neq 0$. So the whole sum equals $p \cdot \#\{f=0\}(\mathbb{F}_p)$, which counts $\mathbb{F}_p$-points of the hypersurface $\{f=0\}$. This suggests that $H^n(X \times \mathbb{A}^1, z \cdot f) \simeq H^{n-2}(\{f=0\})(-1)$ (a Tate-twisted classical motive), consistent with the claim.

item.title: Exponential Motives — Lesson III
item.description:
Recap: Nori Motives

Recall the category of Nori motives $M(k) = \langle Q(k), \rho_B \rangle$, where $Q(k)$ is the quiver of algebraic varieties over $k$ with vertices $[X, Y, n, i]$ and arrows of types (a), (b), (c) inspired by the Kontsevich–Zagier conjecture. The Betti representation is:

$$\rho_B: Q(k) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Vect}_\mathbb{Q}, \qquad [X, Y, n, i] \longmapsto H^n_B(X, Y)(i).$$

Objects of $M(k)$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-vector spaces with a continuous action of $\mathrm{End}(\rho_B)$.

I. Tensor Product on $M(k)$ and the Tannakian Structure

All of the above was formal. The non-formal, genuinely hard part of the construction is:

Theorem (Nori). The category $M(k)$ is equipped with a tensor product $\otimes$, making it into a neutral Tannakian category over $\mathbb{Q}$, with fiber functor the Betti realization:

$$\omega_B: M(k) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Vect}_\mathbb{Q}, \qquad \omega_B([X, Y, n, i]) = H^n_B(X, Y)(i).$$

The theorem says in particular that $\otimes$ in $M(k)$ is compatible with the Künneth formula via $\omega_B$.

Why is this non-trivial? We need to define $[X, Y, n, i] \otimes [X', Y', n', i']$ compatibly with $\rho_B$. The natural candidate is $[X \times X',\, (Y \times X') \cup (X \times Y'),\, n+n',\, i+i']$. The problem is that Künneth gives:

$$H^{n+n'}_B\!\left(X \times X',\, (Y \times X') \cup (X \times Y')\right) \simeq \bigoplus_{\substack{a+b=n+n'}} H^a_B(X, Y) \otimes H^b_B(X', Y'),$$

and there are many pairs $(a,b)$ with $a+b = n+n'$, not just $(n,n')$. Even without Tate twists the naive definition does not work.

Nori solved this using his basic lemma: the idea is to ensure only the pair $(a,b) = (n,n')$ contributes, by an appropriate connectivity/vanishing argument.

Tannakian Structure and the Motivic Galois Group

Being a neutral Tannakian category over $\mathbb{Q}$ means there exists an affine group scheme, the motivic Galois group $G_{\mathrm{mot}}(k)$, such that:

$$M(k) \simeq \mathrm{Rep}(G_{\mathrm{mot}}(k)).$$

This group is enormous — not finite-dimensional at all. From this point of view, a motive is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space with an action of $G_{\mathrm{mot}}(k)$ factoring through a finite-dimensional algebraic quotient.

Remark. The Tate twists are needed precisely to ensure that $G_{\mathrm{mot}}(k)$ is a group: one needs invertible objects under $\otimes$, and $\mathbb{Q}(1) = H^1_B(\mathbb{G}_m)$ with its inverse $\mathbb{Q}(-1)$ provide these. A miracle: adding this single inverse gives all the inverses needed.

II. The Period Torsor and the Kontsevich–Zagier Conjecture

The De Rham Realization

Periods come from the comparison isomorphism, but $M(k)$ so far only uses $\omega_B$. To access periods, we need a second functor.

Using the universal property of Nori's construction, one builds a de Rham realization functor:

$$\omega_{\mathrm{dR}}: M(k) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Vect}_k,$$

such that when $X$ is smooth and $Y$ is s.n.c.:

$$\omega_{\mathrm{dR}}([X, Y, n, i]) = H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, Y)(i).$$

The two realization functors fit in the following diagram:

The Period Torsor $\mathcal{P}$

Comparing the two realization functors, one defines the period torsor:

$$\mathcal{P} = \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}^{\otimes}(\omega_{\mathrm{dR}},\, \omega_B \otimes_\mathbb{Q} k),$$

the affine $k$-scheme parametrizing tensor-compatible isomorphisms between the two realizations. One proves this functor of points is representable.

This may look abstract, but we know a concrete complex point of $\mathcal{P}$: the Grothendieck comparison isomorphism

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, Y) \otimes_k \mathbb{C} \xrightarrow{\sim} H^*_B(X, Y) \otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{C}$$

gives an element $\mathrm{comp} \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{C})$. So $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{C}) \neq \emptyset$, which implies $\mathcal{P} \neq \emptyset$ as a scheme.

Periods as Functions on $\mathcal{P}$

Regular functions on $\mathcal{P}$ can be evaluated at $\mathrm{comp}$:

$$\mathcal{O}\!\left(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}^{\otimes}(\omega_{\mathrm{dR}},\, \omega_B \otimes k)\right) \xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{ev}_{\mathrm{comp}}\;} \mathbb{C}.$$
Conjecture (Kontsevich–Zagier). This evaluation map is injective.

Remark. The image is exactly the ring of periods, by definition — the three relations (bilinearity, change of variables, Stokes) used to define equality of periods are precisely the relations used to define the morphisms in $Q(k)$, built into the structure of $M(k)$.

Explicit Description

Given $[\omega] \in H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, Y)$ and $[\sigma] \in H^B_n(X, Y)$, these define an object $H^n(X, Y) \in M(k)$ and a regular function on $\mathcal{P}$:

$$\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}^{\otimes}(\omega_{\mathrm{dR}},\, \omega_B \otimes k) \longrightarrow \mathbb{A}^1_k, \qquad \varphi \longmapsto \langle \varphi_{H^n(X,Y)}([\omega]),\, [\sigma] \rangle.$$

Here $\varphi = (\varphi_M)_{M \in \mathrm{Ob}(M(k))}$ and we take the component at $H^n(X,Y)$. When $\varphi = \mathrm{comp}$, this gives exactly $\int_\sigma \omega$.

Alternative viewpoint. The comparison isomorphism is a generic point of $\mathcal{P}$.

Toy example. Take $k = \mathbb{Q}$, $X = \mathbb{A}^1_\mathbb{Q}$, so $\mathcal{O}(X) = \mathbb{Q}[x]$. A point $\alpha \in X(\mathbb{C}) = \mathbb{C}$ gives:

$$\mathbb{Q}[x] \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}, \qquad P \longmapsto P(\alpha).$$

This is injective $\iff$ $\alpha$ is transcendental $\iff$ $\alpha$ is a generic point of $\mathbb{A}^1_\mathbb{Q}$. The conjecture asserts that $\mathrm{comp}$ is a generic point of $\mathcal{P}$ (and in particular $\mathcal{P}$ should be irreducible).

Working Object by Object

$G_{\mathrm{mot}}(k)$ is too large to study directly. Given $M \in M(k)$, consider the smallest Tannakian subcategory $\langle M \rangle^{\otimes} \subset M(k)$ containing $M$. By Tannaka duality $\langle M \rangle^{\otimes} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}(G_M)$ where $G_M$ fits into:

Grothendieck Period Conjecture. For $X$ smooth and $Y \subset X$ s.n.c.:

$$\mathrm{tr.deg}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}\!\left(\text{periods of } H^n(X, Y)\right) = \dim_\mathbb{Q} G_{H^n(X,Y)}.$$

Putting everything together, this conjecture is equivalent to the Kontsevich–Zagier conjecture.

III. Cohomology Theories for Varieties with a Function

Motivation

We have said that there are numbers not expected to be periods:

$$e^\alpha \text{ for } \alpha \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}^\times, \qquad \sqrt{\pi} = \Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-x^2}\,dx, \qquad \gamma = \iint_{\substack{x \geq 0,\, y \leq 1}} e^{-xy}\,dx\,dy.$$

The current state of knowledge is very poor: we do not know 3 periods that are algebraically independent, the transcendence degree of the ring of periods could conceivably be as small as 2, and we do not know a single explicit non-period. The numbers above are only conjectured to not be periods.

Setup

Let $k \subset \mathbb{C}$, $X$ smooth over $k$, and $f \in \mathcal{O}_X(X)$ a regular function, i.e. a morphism $X \xrightarrow{f} \mathbb{A}^1_k$. If $f$ is non-constant, $X$ is not proper. We want to consider integrals $\int_\sigma e^{-f}\omega$, which should satisfy a Stokes formula. Indeed:

$$d(e^{-f}\omega) = e^{-f}(d\omega - df \wedge \omega).$$

Twisted de Rham Cohomology

Definition. The twisted de Rham cohomology of $(X, f)$ is:

$$H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X; f) := \mathbb{H}^n_{\mathrm{Zar}}\!\left(X,\; \mathcal{O}_X \xrightarrow{d_f} \Omega^1_X \xrightarrow{d_f} \Omega^2_X \xrightarrow{d_f} \cdots\right),$$

where the twisted differential is $d_f(\omega) := d\omega - df \wedge \omega$.

This is indeed a complex: $d_f^2 = 0$ because $d_f = e^f \circ d \circ e^{-f}$, so $d_f^2 = e^f \circ d^2 \circ e^{-f} = 0$.

Remark. If $f$ is constant: $H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X; f) = H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)$. Classical motives are a special case with $f = 0$.

Conceptual Explanation: Vector Bundles with Connection

Twisted de Rham cohomology is the de Rham cohomology of a vector bundle with integrable connection: a morphism

satisfying the Leibniz rule: $\nabla(g \cdot e) = e \otimes dg + g \cdot \nabla(e)$.

The trivial connection is $\mathcal{E} = \mathcal{O}_X$, $\nabla(1) = 0$, giving the usual de Rham complex $\mathcal{O}_X \xrightarrow{d} \Omega^1_X$.

In our case, $\mathcal{E} = \mathcal{O}_X$ with the twisted connection:

$$\nabla_f(1) = -df, \qquad \nabla_f(g) = dg - g\,df \quad \text{for } g \in \mathcal{O}_X.$$

The associated de Rham complex is exactly $(\Omega^\bullet_X, d_f)$.

Analytification and the Poincaré Lemma

On $X^{\mathrm{an}}$, consider the analytic horizontal sections $\ker(\nabla_f^{\mathrm{an}}) \subset \mathcal{O}_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}$.

Poincaré Lemma.

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR,an}}(X^{\mathrm{an}},\, f^{\mathrm{an}}) \simeq H^*(X^{\mathrm{an}},\, \ker(\nabla_f^{\mathrm{an}})).$$

In the trivial case: $\ker(\nabla^{\mathrm{an}}) = \underline{\mathbb{C}}_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}$ (constant sheaf). In the twisted case: a holomorphic $g$ satisfies $\nabla_f^{\mathrm{an}}(g) = 0 \iff dg = g\,df \iff g = c\cdot e^f$, so $\ker(\nabla_f^{\mathrm{an}}) = \mathbb{C}\cdot e^f \cong \underline{\mathbb{C}}_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}$.

Upshot. $H^*_{\mathrm{dR,an}}(X^{\mathrm{an}}, f^{\mathrm{an}}) \simeq H^*(X(\mathbb{C}), \mathbb{C})$ = usual singular cohomology of $X(\mathbb{C})$. This is a manifestation of the phenomenon of irregular singularities: algebraically the twisted cohomology can be very different from the classical one, but analytically it recovers the usual topology.

Example: $X = \mathbb{A}^1_k$, $f = x^n$, $n \geq 2$

Since $X$ is affine, hypercohomology reduces to the complex of global sections:

$$k[x] \xrightarrow{d_f} k[x]\,dx, \qquad P \longmapsto (P' - nx^{n-1}P)\,dx.$$

Degree 0. $H^0_{\mathrm{dR}}(X; f) = \ker(d_f) = 0$: the only solution of $P' = nx^{n-1}P$ is $P = c\cdot e^{x^n}$, which is not a polynomial.

Degree 1. $H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X; f) = \mathrm{coker}(d_f)$. The classes $dx, x\,dx, \ldots, x^{n-2}\,dx$ are linearly independent in the cokernel. To see they span, use algebraic integration by parts:

$$d_f\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{n}\right) = -nx^{n-1}\,dx \implies x^{n-1}\,dx = 0,$$

$$d_f\!\left(-\tfrac{x}{n}\right) = x^n\,dx - \tfrac{1}{n}\,dx \implies x^n\,dx = \tfrac{1}{n}\,dx,$$

$$d_f\!\left(-\tfrac{x^2}{n}\right) = x^{n+1}\,dx - \tfrac{2}{n}\,x\,dx \implies x^{n+1}\,dx = \tfrac{2}{n}\,x\,dx,$$

and by induction every $x^j\,dx$ for $j \geq n-1$ is in the span of $\{dx, \ldots, x^{n-2}\,dx\}$. Therefore:

$$H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^1_k;\, x^n) \cong k[dx] \oplus k[x\,dx] \oplus \cdots \oplus k[x^{n-2}\,dx], \quad \dim = n-1.$$

Exercise. Show that $H^1_{\mathrm{dR,an}}(\mathbb{A}^1_\mathbb{C};\, x^n) = 0$ (any holomorphic 1-form is in the image of $d_f$). This confirms the Poincaré lemma, since $\mathbb{C}$ is contractible.

IV. Rapid Decay Homology

We want to integrate $e^{-f}\omega$ over chains, but convergence requires $e^{-f}$ to decay on the non-compact ends.

Setup

Define the right half-planes in $\mathbb{C}$:

$$S_r = \{z \in \mathbb{C} \mid \mathrm{Re}(z) > r\}, \qquad r \in \mathbb{R}.$$

On the preimage $f^{-1}(S_r(\mathbb{C})) \subset X(\mathbb{C})$ the function $e^{-f}$ decays exponentially.

Proposition. There exists a Zariski open $U \subset \mathbb{A}^1_k$ (the set of non-critical values, by Ehresmann's theorem) such that $f^{-1}(U(\mathbb{C})) \xrightarrow{f} U(\mathbb{C})$ is a locally trivial fibration: for every $x \in U(\mathbb{C})$, there exists an open $V_x \ni x$ such that $f^{-1}(x) \hookrightarrow f^{-1}(V_x)$ is a homotopy equivalence.

In particular, for $r$ large enough the transition maps in the system $(H^{\mathrm{sing}}_n(X(\mathbb{C}), f^{-1}(S_r)))_{r \to +\infty}$ are isomorphisms.

Definition (Rapid Decay Homology).

$$H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_n(X, f) := \varinjlim_{r \to +\infty} H^{\mathrm{sing}}_n\!\left(X(\mathbb{C}),\, f^{-1}(S_r);\, \mathbb{Q}\right), \qquad S_r = \{\mathrm{Re}(z) > r\}.$$

Summary. An element of $H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_n(X, f)$ is (for $r$ large enough) a chain $\sigma$ in $X(\mathbb{C})$ whose boundary lies in $f^{-1}(S_r) = \{\mathrm{Re}(f) > r\}$. Two chains are identified if they agree for all large $r$.

Special cases.

  • If $f$ is constant, the image lies in a single point, so $f^{-1}(S_r) = \emptyset$ for large $r$ and $H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_n(X, f) = H^B_n(X)$ (usual Betti homology).
  • The integral $\int_\sigma e^{-f}\omega$ converges for $\sigma \in H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_n(X, f)$, since $e^{-f}$ is exponentially small on $\{\mathrm{Re}(f) > r\}$.

Example: $X = \mathbb{A}^1_k$, $f = x^n$

The region $\{\mathrm{Re}(x^n) > r\}$ in $\mathbb{C}$ consists of $n$ Stokes sectors, separated by the anti-Stokes directions at angles $\frac{(2j+1)\pi}{n}$ for $j = 0, \ldots, n-1$. Each sector is a connected component where $|e^{-x^n}|$ decays as $|x| \to \infty$.

We have $H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_1(\mathbb{A}^1, x^n) \cong H^B_1(\mathbb{C}, \{n\text{ points}\})$, which has dimension $n-1$. A set of $n-1$ generators consists of paths connecting adjacent sectors at infinity (each path goes to $\infty$ inside those sectors, so has boundary in the rapid decay region). For $n = 2$: the single generator is the path along $\mathbb{R}$ from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$.

Integrating $e^{-x^n}\,dx$ along these cycles gives values proportional to $\Gamma(1/n)$ (via $t = x^n$):

$$\int_\sigma e^{-x^n}\,dx \sim \Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{1}{n}\right).$$

This gives the comparison isomorphism between $H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^1; x^n)$ (of dimension $n-1$) and $H^{\mathrm{Rd}}_1(\mathbb{A}^1, x^n)$ (also of dimension $n-1$), with period matrix entries the values $\Gamma(j/n)$ for $j = 1, \ldots, n-1$.

item.title: Exponential Motives — Lesson II
item.description:
Recall from last time: for $k \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ and $X$ a smooth algebraic variety over $k$, the comparison isomorphism gives

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X) \otimes_k \mathbb{C} \xrightarrow{\sim} H^*_B(X) \otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{C}, \qquad [\omega] \longmapsto \left([\sigma] \mapsto \int_\sigma \omega\right).$$

The preliminary definition of a period was: any number of the form $\int_\sigma \omega$, whenever $k \subset \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.

Why preliminary? Because we would also like numbers such as

$$\log 2 = \int_1^2 \frac{dx}{x} = \int_\sigma \omega,$$

but here $\partial\sigma \neq 0$: the chain $\sigma = [1,2]$ has boundary $2 - 1 \neq 0$, so it is not a cycle.

Solution: use relative cohomology. We allow chains with non-trivial boundary, as long as the boundary is contained in a fixed subvariety.

I. Relative Cohomology

Let $Y \hookrightarrow X$ be a closed subvariety defined over $k$.

Betti Side

Definition. The relative Betti cohomology $H^*_B(X, Y)$ is the dual of the relative singular homology

$$H^B_*(X, Y) := H^{\mathrm{sing}}_*(X(\mathbb{C}), Y(\mathbb{C}),\, \mathbb{Q}),$$

which is the homology of the cone of the chain map $i_*: C_*(Y(\mathbb{C})) \to C_*(X(\mathbb{C}))$.

The map $i_*$ is injective (just composing a simplex in $Y$ with the inclusion), and the cone complex is:

$$\bigl(\mathrm{Cone}(i_*)\bigr)_n = C_{n-1}(Y(\mathbb{C})) \oplus C_n(X(\mathbb{C}))$$

with differential $\partial(a, b) = \bigl(-\partial a,\; \partial b + i_*(a)\bigr)$ for $a \in C_{n-1}(Y(\mathbb{C}))$, $b \in C_n(X(\mathbb{C}))$.

So concretely, an element of $H^B_n(X, Y)$ is represented by a pair $(\sigma_Y, \sigma_X)$ which is closed:

$$\partial \sigma_Y = 0, \qquad \partial \sigma_X + i_*(\sigma_Y) = 0.$$

Since $i_*$ is injective, this simplifies: you just need $\sigma_X$ with $\partial(\sigma_X) \in C_{n-1}(Y(\mathbb{C}))$.

This is exactly what we wanted: the boundary of $\sigma_X$ must lie in $Y(\mathbb{C})$.

By design, the construction gives a long exact sequence:

$$\cdots \to H^B_n(Y) \xrightarrow{i_*} H^B_n(X) \longrightarrow H^B_n(X,Y) \xrightarrow{\partial} H^B_{n-1}(Y) \to \cdots$$

So knowing the homology of $X$ and $Y$ at least controls the dimensions of the relative groups.

In terms of sheaves. Writing $Y \overset{i}{\hookrightarrow} X \overset{j}{\hookleftarrow} X\setminus Y$ (closed/open), one has

$$H^*_B(X, Y) \simeq H^*\!\left(X^{\mathrm{an}},\, j_! j^* \underline{\mathbb{Q}}_X\right).$$

There is a short exact sequence of sheaves

$$0 \longrightarrow j_! j^* \underline{\mathbb{Q}}_X \longrightarrow \underline{\mathbb{Q}}_X \longrightarrow i_* \underline{\mathbb{Q}}_Y \longrightarrow 0,$$

which gives exactly the long exact sequence above.

De Rham Side

Assume $Y$ is smooth. The closed immersion $i: Y \hookrightarrow X$ induces a morphism of de Rham complexes:

$$\Omega^\bullet_X \xrightarrow{i^*} i_* \Omega^\bullet_Y.$$

We now take the total complex $\mathrm{Tot}(i^*)$ of the double complex

$$\begin{array}{ccccc} \vdots & & \vdots \\ \Omega^2_X & \longrightarrow & i_*\Omega^2_Y \\ \uparrow & & \uparrow \\ \Omega^1_X & \longrightarrow & i_*\Omega^1_Y \\ \uparrow & & \uparrow \\ \mathcal{O}_X & \longrightarrow & i_*\mathcal{O}_Y \end{array}$$

and look at the diagonal. The total complex $\mathrm{Tot}(i^*)$ has differential

$$d(a,b) = \bigl(da,\; -db + i^*a\bigr), \qquad a \in \Omega^n_X,\; b \in i_*\Omega^{n-1}_Y.$$

Definition.

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, Y) := \mathbb{H}^*_{\mathrm{Zar}}\!\left(X,\, \mathrm{Tot}(i^*)\right) \qquad \text{(hypercohomology)}.$$

Concretely (assuming $X$ affine, so global sections suffice): a class in $H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, Y)$ is represented by a pair

$$\omega_X \in \Omega^n_X(X) \quad \text{with} \quad d\omega_X = 0,$$

$$\eta_Y \in \Omega^{n-1}_Y(Y) \quad \text{with} \quad \omega_X\big|_Y = d\eta_Y.$$

The map $[(\omega_X, \eta_Y)] \mapsto [\omega_X]$ (forgetting $\eta_Y$) fits into the long exact sequence by design:

$$\cdots \longrightarrow H^{n-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(Y) \longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, Y) \longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X) \longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(Y) \longrightarrow \cdots$$

Example: $X = \mathbb{A}^1_\mathbb{Q} \setminus \{0\}$, $Y = \{1, 2\}$

Take $X = \mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Q}[x, x^{-1}])$ (which is the right setting for $\frac{dx}{x}$) and $Y = \{1, 2\} = \{(x-1)(x-2) = 0\}$.

De Rham computation. The total complex of $i^*$ is:

$$\mathbb{Q}[x, x^{-1}] \longrightarrow \mathbb{Q}[x, x^{-1}]\,dx \;\oplus\; \mathbb{Q} \oplus \mathbb{Q}$$

$$P \longmapsto \bigl(P'(x)\,dx,\; P(1),\; P(2)\bigr)$$

(restriction to $Y$ is just evaluation; the rest of the complex is zero). Thus $H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, Y)$ is the cohomology of this map. We find the cokernel (things not in the image):

  • $\bigl(\frac{dx}{x}, 0, 0\bigr)$: certainly not in the image, since the logarithm is not algebraic.
  • $(0, 1, 0)$: not in the image either — if $P' = 0$ then $P$ is constant, so $P(1)$ must equal $P(2)$.

These two are linearly independent in the cokernel.

Exercise. Show that they form a basis.

Moreover, $(0, 1, 0)$ defines the same class as $\bigl(\frac{dx}{x}, 0, 0\bigr)$. Indeed, their difference

$$\left(\frac{dx}{x}, 0, 0\right) - (0, 1, 0) = \left(\frac{dx}{x}, -1, 0\right)$$

lies in the image: we need $P$ with $P' = 1$, $P(1) = -1$, $P(2) = 0$. Since $P' = 1 \Rightarrow P = x + c$, the system $1 + c = -1$, $2 + c = 0$ gives $c = -2$. So it is the image of $P(x) = x - 2$. Therefore:

$$H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}\!\left(\mathbb{A}^1_\mathbb{Q} \setminus \{0\},\; \{1,2\}\right) = \mathbb{Q}\bigl[dx\bigr] \oplus \mathbb{Q}\!\left[\tfrac{dx}{x}\right].$$

Betti computation. We have $X(\mathbb{C}) = \mathbb{C}^*$ and $Y(\mathbb{C}) = \{1, 2\}$. The relevant piece of the long exact sequence is:

$$0 \to H^B_1(X) \to H^B_1(X, Y) \xrightarrow{\partial} H^B_0(Y) \to H^B_0(X) \to 0$$

$$\| \qquad\qquad\quad \| \qquad\qquad\qquad\quad \| \qquad\qquad\quad \|$$

$$\mathbb{Q}\cdot\gamma \qquad \bullet\!\to\!\bullet \qquad\quad \mathbb{Q} \oplus \mathbb{Q} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{sum}} \mathbb{Q}$$

The two generators of $H^B_1(X, Y)$ are: $\gamma$ (the loop $|x|=1$ around $0$) and the path from $1$ to $2$.

Period matrix. Integrating the two de Rham classes against the two Betti classes:

$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & dx & \dfrac{dx}{x} \\[6pt] \hline [1 \to 2] & 1 & \log 2 \\[6pt] \gamma & 0 & 2\pi i \end{array}$$

Theorem. There is a comparison isomorphism

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X, Y) \otimes_k \mathbb{C} \xrightarrow{\sim} H^*_B(X, Y) \otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{C},$$

dual to the relative period pairing:

$$[(\omega_X, \eta_Y)] \otimes [\sigma_X] \longmapsto \int_{\sigma_X} \omega_X + \int_{\partial \sigma_X} \eta_Y.$$

Remark. This is still not enough in general: we need to extend to the case where $Y$ is not smooth, but merely has simple normal crossing (s.n.c.) singularities. (This is needed precisely because the compactification used in the proof of the comparison isomorphism only produces s.n.c. divisors.)

The (Final) Definition of a Period

Definition. A period is a coefficient of the comparison isomorphism for some $H^n(X, Y)$ over $k \subset \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, where $X$ is smooth and $Y$ is a simple normal crossing divisor.

Goal. Attach to any period a motivic Galois group. This requires understanding all algebraic relations between periods. That is: given periods $p_1, \ldots, p_r$, find all $Q \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}[x_1, \ldots, x_r]$ with $Q(p_1, \ldots, p_r) = 0$.

Remark. It is enough to understand equality between periods. Indeed, periods form a $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-algebra (closed under $+$ and $\cdot$, containing $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$), so any polynomial relation reduces to checking whether a given period equals zero.

Key point: Künneth formula. For both cohomologies (both de Rham and Betti, when not stated otherwise):

$$H^*(X_1, Y_1) \otimes H^*(X_2, Y_2) \simeq H^*\!\left(X_1 \times X_2,\; (Y_1 \times X_2) \cup (X_1 \times Y_2)\right).$$

Thus we just need to understand equality of periods. There are three sources of relations:

  1. Bilinearity of the period pairing: integrating over a sum of cycles is the sum of the integrals, both over cycles and over forms.

  2. Change of variables: for a morphism $f: X \to X'$,

    $$\int_\sigma f^*\omega = \int_{f_*\sigma} \omega.$$

  3. Stokes' formula:

    $$\int_\sigma d\omega = \int_{\partial\sigma} \omega.$$

    Note: in the relative context, $\partial\sigma$ is no longer necessarily zero.

Conjecture (Kontsevich–Zagier). Any relation between periods follows from these three.

In other words: if you have an equality between two periods, you can derive it by applying only these three types of relations. This will be made more formal later.

II. Nori Motives

Inspired by the Kontsevich–Zagier conjecture, Nori's construction gives one of the ways to define motives. The key feature is that we can define the motivic Galois group unconditionally; the conjecture then implies that it acts on periods (on all of them). Conjecturally, these groups are the Galois group of periods in a precise sense.

Quivers and Representations

Definition. A quiver is a directed graph — think of it as a category without composition (composition will be added later).

Definition. A representation of a quiver $Q$ is a functor $\rho: Q \to \mathrm{Vect}_\mathbb{Q}$: to each vertex a vector space, and to each arrow a linear map.

The Endomorphism Algebra

Given a representation $\rho: Q \to \mathrm{Vect}_\mathbb{Q}$, define:

$$\mathrm{End}(\rho) = \varprojlim_{\substack{Q_0 \subseteq Q \\ \text{finite}}} \mathrm{End}\!\left(\rho\big|_{Q_0}\right),$$

where the limit runs over all finite sub-quivers $Q_0$. This is a $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra with a natural topology inherited as a limit of finite-dimensional algebras.

For a fixed finite $Q_0$, we define:

$$\mathrm{End}\!\left(\rho\big|_{Q_0}\right) = \left\{(e_q)_{q \in Q_0} \in \prod_{q \in Q_0} \mathrm{End}(\rho(q)) \;\middle|\; \text{compatible}\right\},$$

where compatible means: for every arrow $f: q \to q'$ in $Q_0$, the diagram

$$\begin{array}{ccc} \rho(q) & \xrightarrow{\rho(f)} & \rho(q') \\ e_q \downarrow & & \downarrow e_{q'} \\ \rho(q) & \xrightarrow{\rho(f)} & \rho(q') \end{array}$$

commutes. Therefore $\mathrm{End}(\rho)$ is a pro-finite-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra.

Definition. $\langle Q, \rho \rangle$ is the category of finite-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-vector spaces with a continuous action of $\mathrm{End}(\rho)$.

An object of $\langle Q, \rho \rangle$ is a vector space $V$ together with a ring map $\mathrm{End}(\rho) \to \mathrm{End}(V)$ that factors through $\mathrm{End}(\rho|_{Q_0})$ for some finite $Q_0$ — i.e., the action is continuous for the profinite topology. There are natural "functors" assembling into:

$$Q \xrightarrow{\rho} \mathrm{Vect}_\mathbb{Q} \qquad \text{and} \qquad Q \to \langle Q, \rho \rangle \xrightarrow{\text{forgetful}} \mathrm{Vect}_\mathbb{Q}, \quad q \mapsto \rho(q).$$

Proposition (Nori) — Universal property. The construction $\langle Q, \rho \rangle$ is universal: whenever $\mathcal{A}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear abelian category and $\beta: \mathcal{A} \to \mathrm{Vect}_\mathbb{Q}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear exact faithful functor, any factorization of $\rho$ through $\mathcal{A}$ induces a unique (up to unique isomorphism) functor $\langle Q, \rho \rangle \to \mathcal{A}$:

$$\begin{array}{ccc} & & \mathcal{A} \\ & \nearrow & \downarrow \beta \\ Q & \xrightarrow{\rho} & \mathrm{Vect}_\mathbb{Q} \end{array}$$

The Nori Quiver $Q(k)$

We apply the above to the specific quiver $Q(k)$:

Vertices: symbols $[X, Y, n, i]$ where $X$ is a variety over $k$, $Y \subset X$ is closed, and $n, i \in \mathbb{Z}$ (with $n$ the cohomological degree and $i$ the Tate twist). Morally, the vertex $[X, Y, n, i]$ corresponds to $H^n(X, Y)$ with Tate twist $(i)$.

Arrows (three types, each inspired by one of the three sources of relations):

  • Type (a): For every morphism $h: X \to X'$ with $h(Y) \subset Y'$, a functoriality arrow:

    $$[X', Y', n, i] \xrightarrow{h^*} [X, Y, n, i].$$

  • Type (b): For every $Z \subset Y \subset X$ closed, a connecting homomorphism:

    $$[Y, Z, n-1, i] \xrightarrow{\partial} [X, Y, n, i].$$

  • Type (c): For every $Y \subset X$ closed, a Tate/Künneth arrow:

    $$\left[X \times \mathbb{G}_m,\; (Y \times \mathbb{G}_m) \cup (X \times \{1\}),\; n+1,\; i+1\right] \longrightarrow [X, Y, n, i].$$

The Quiver Representation $\rho_B$

The Betti representation is:

$$\rho_B: Q(k) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Vect}_\mathbb{Q}, \qquad [X, Y, n, i] \longmapsto H^n_B(X, Y)(i),$$

where the Tate twist $(i)$ means tensoring $(-i)$ times with

$$H^1_B(\mathbb{G}_m) \simeq H^1_B(\mathbb{G}_m, \{1\}) = \mathbb{Q}(-1).$$

Concretely: for $i > 0$, tensor $i$ times; for $i < 0$, tensor $(-i)$ times with the dual.

The arrows are mapped as follows:

  • (a): $H^n_B(X', Y')(i) \xrightarrow{h^*} H^n_B(X, Y)(i)$.
  • (b): $H^{n-1}_B(Y, Z)(i) \xrightarrow{\partial} H^n_B(X, Y)(i)$.
  • (c): By the Künneth formula: $$H^{n+1}_B\!\bigl(X \times \mathbb{G}_m,\; (Y \times \mathbb{G}_m) \cup (X \times \{1\})\bigr)(i+1) \;=\; \bigoplus_{a+b=n+1} H^a_B(X,Y) \otimes H^b_B(\mathbb{G}_m, 1) \cdot (i+1).$$ Since $H^b_B(\mathbb{G}_m, 1) = 0$ for $b \neq 1$ and $= H^1_B(\mathbb{G}_m)$ for $b = 1$ (because $\mathbb{G}_m = \mathbb{C}^*$ is connected, so $H^0 \simeq \mathbb{Q}$, and taking the relative group with respect to $\{1\}$ kills it), this collapses to $\simeq H^n_B(X, Y)(i)$, giving the required isomorphism.

The Category of Nori Motives

To have a category with duals, one formally introduces the dual via the Tate twist (the sign convention $-i$ in the twist). Then:

Definition (Nori Motives). The category of Nori motives over $k$ is

$$M(k) = \langle Q(k),\; \rho_B \rangle.$$

Remark. $M(k)$ is an abelian category. A Nori motive "is" a $H^n_B(X, Y)(i)$, or whatever one can obtain from these by taking kernels, cokernels, and extensions.

We will see informally that $M(k)$ has a tensor product $\otimes$, making it equivalent to the category of representations of a pro-algebraic group — the motivic Galois group.

Relation with Voevodsky Motives

There exists a functor from the derived category $D^b(M(k))$ to Voevodsky's triangulated category of motives $DM(k)$, and conjecturally this functor is an equivalence. So Voevodsky motives should be the derived category of Nori motives.

item.title: Exponential Motives — Lesson I
item.description:
These are notes from a lecture by J. Fresán on Exponential Motives, a generalisation of the theory of motives. There are many ways to think about motives; the perspective here is close to Nori motives, since periods are central.

References:

  • Une introduction aux périodes (has examples)
  • Multiple zeta values: from numbers to motives, Ch. 2
  • Periods and Nori Motives (about Nori)

I. Periods

Let $k \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a subfield of the complex numbers. The most interesting cases are $k = \mathbb{Q}$ or $k = \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.

Let $X$ be a smooth algebraic variety over $k$. Most of the time we assume $X$ is affine. We attach to $X$ two vector spaces over $k$:

a) Algebraic de Rham Cohomology

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X) = \bigoplus_{n \geq 0} H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)$$

This is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space.

b) Betti Cohomology

$$H^*_B(X) = \bigoplus_{n \geq 0} H^n_B(X)$$

This is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space. (This uses the fact that $k \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}$; the de Rham side does not.)

c) Comparison Isomorphism

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X) \otimes_k \mathbb{C} \xrightarrow{\sim} H^*_B(X) \otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{C}$$

Algebraic de Rham Cohomology

On $X$ we have $\Omega^1_{X/k}$, the sheaf of Kähler differentials. Think of it as the algebraic analogue of differential forms on a smooth manifold: locally you have generators $dx_i$, and you can define 1-forms $f_i\, dx_i$ where the $f_i$ are now algebraic (rather than $C^\infty$) functions.

Fact. If $X$ is smooth, then $\Omega^1_{X/k}$ is locally free (hence coherent).

We form the algebraic de Rham complex (a complex of coherent sheaves in the Zariski topology):

$$\mathcal{O}_X \xrightarrow{d} \Omega^1_{X/k} \longrightarrow \Omega^2_{X/k} \longrightarrow \cdots \qquad \text{where } \Omega^p_{X/k} = \wedge^p \Omega^1_{X/k}.$$

Denote this complex $\Omega^\bullet_{X/k}$.

Definition.

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X) := \mathbb{H}^*_{\mathrm{Zar}}(X,\, \Omega^\bullet_{X/k})$$

(hypercohomology of that complex of sheaves).

Remark. There is a spectral sequence

$$E_1^{p,q} = H^q(X,\, \Omega^p_X) \Rightarrow H^{p+q}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X).$$

Remark (affine case). If $X$ is affine, coherent sheaves have no positive cohomology, so $H^q(X, \Omega^p_X) = 0$ for all $q \geq 1$. The spectral sequence degenerates at the first page, and therefore:

$$H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X) = H^n\!\left(\mathcal{O}_X(X) \to \Omega^1_X(X) \to \Omega^2_X(X) \to \cdots\right)$$

i.e. the cohomology of the complex of global sections. This is finite-dimensional. In particular, an element of $H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)$ is the class $[\omega]$ of some $\omega \in \Omega^n_X(X)$ with $d\omega = 0$ (closed).

Remark. If $X$ is not affine, it is not easy to write explicit examples of forms. One usually passes through hypercohomology. For instance, if $X = \bigcup_i U_i$ is a union of affines, an element of $H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)$ looks like a tuple

$$\left([\omega_{U_i}]_{U_i},\ [\eta_{U_i \cap U_j}]_{U_i \cap U_j},\ \ldots\right).$$

Exercise. Try this for $\mathbb{P}^1$, which has 2 affine opens.

Betti Cohomology (= Singular Cohomology)

("Betti" is standard terminology in algebraic geometry.)

Since $k \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}$, we can consider

$$X(\mathbb{C}) = \mathrm{Hom}_k(\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{C},\, X).$$

This is a nice topological space — in fact a complex manifold (because $X$ is smooth). So we can take singular cohomology:

$$H^*_B(X) := H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X(\mathbb{C}),\, \mathbb{Q}) = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Vect}_\mathbb{Q}}\!\left(H^B_*(X),\, \mathbb{Q}\right).$$

We work with $\mathbb{Q}$-coefficients: by the universal coefficient theorem, $H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X(\mathbb{C}), \mathbb{Q})$ is exactly the $\mathbb{Q}$-dual of the singular homology $H^B_*(X)$.

Recall singular homology:

$$C_p(X(\mathbb{C})) = \bigoplus_{\sigma:\Delta^p \to X(\mathbb{C})} \mathbb{Q} \cdot \sigma, \qquad \Delta^p = \{(x_0,\ldots,x_p)\in\mathbb{R}^{p+1} : x_i \geq 0,\ \textstyle\sum x_i = 1\}.$$

The boundary maps are given by the alternating sum of face inclusions $\partial_i: \Delta^{p-1} \to \Delta^p$. An element of $H^B_n(X(\mathbb{C}))$ is a class $[\sigma]$ of some $\sigma: \Delta^n \to X(\mathbb{C})$ with $\partial\sigma = 0$.

Proposition.

  1. The homology does not change if we restrict to $C^\infty$-simplices, i.e. there exists an open neighbourhood $U$ of $\Delta^n$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ such that any $\sigma: \Delta^n \to X(\mathbb{C})$ extends to a $C^\infty$-function $\tilde\sigma: U \to X(\mathbb{C})$.
  2. $H^*_B(X)$ agrees with sheaf cohomology: $H^*(X(\mathbb{C}),\, \underline{\mathbb{Q}}_{X(\mathbb{C})})$, where $\underline{\mathbb{Q}}_{X(\mathbb{C})}$ is the constant sheaf of locally constant functions.

The De Rham–Grothendieck Theorem

Theorem (De Rham, Grothendieck). There is a canonical isomorphism

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X) \otimes_k \mathbb{C} \xrightarrow{\sim} H^*_B(X) \otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{C},$$

which is dual to a perfect pairing:

$$H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X) \otimes H^B_*(X) \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}.$$

This pairing is uniquely determined by what it does on affine varieties. On an affine $X$, it is given by:

$$[\omega] \otimes [\sigma] \longmapsto \int_\sigma \omega,$$

where for $\sigma = \sum n_i \sigma_i$ with $\sigma_i: \Delta^n \to X(\mathbb{C})$, we set $\int_\sigma \omega = \sum n_i \int_{\Delta^n} \sigma_i^*(\omega)$.

Remark. The pairing is well-defined and independent of the choice of representatives: $\int_\sigma d\eta = \int_{\partial\sigma} \eta = 0$, and similarly changing $\omega$ by an exact form gives zero.

Remark. Note that tensoring with $k$ is not enough — one needs $\mathbb{C}$! Indeed, $H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)$ and $H^*_B(X)$ are isomorphic over $\mathbb{Q}$ (as abstract vector spaces of the same dimension), but the only way to write down the isomorphism is over $\mathbb{C}$.

The isomorphism is canonical, meaning it is functorial: given a morphism $f: X \to Y$ of algebraic varieties over $k$, the diagram
